title: Getting Started with pomdp
text: R package pomdp (Hahsler Cassandra 2025),(Hahsler 2025) provides infrastructure define analyze solutions Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDP) models. package companion package pomdpSolve provides executable ‘pomdp-solve’ (Cassandra 2015), well-known fast C implementation variety algorithms solve POMDPs. pomdp can also use package sarsop (Boettiger et al. 2021) provides implementation SARSOP (Successive Approximations Reachable Space Optimal Policies) algorithm. package provides following algorithms: Exact value iteration Enumeration algorithm (Sondik 1971). Two pass algorithm (Sondik 1971). Witness algorithm (Littman et al. 1995). Incremental pruning algorithm (Zhang Liu 1996), (Cassandra et al. 1997). Approximate value iteration Finite grid algorithm (Cassandra 2015), variation point-based value iteration solve larger POMDPs (PBVI; see (Pineau et al. 2003)) without dynamic belief set expansion. SARSOP (Kurniawati et al. 2008), Successive Approximations Reachable Space Optimal Policies, point-based algorithm approximates optimally reachable belief spaces infinite-horizon problems (via package sarsop (Boettiger et al. 2021)). package enables user simply define components POMDP model solve problem using several methods. package also contains functions analyze visualize POMDP solutions (e.g., optimal policy) extends regular MDPs. document, give brief introduction concept POMDPs, describe features R package, illustrate usage toy example.

title: Getting Started with pomdp
text: demonstrate use package Tiger Problem (Cassandra et al. 1994). problem defined : agent facing two closed doors tiger put equal probability behind one two doors represented states tiger-left tiger-right, treasure put behind door. possible actions listen tiger noises opening door (actions open-left open-right). title: Infrastructure for Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDP)
text: partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) models agent’s decision process agent directly observe environment’s state rely observations. goal find optimal policy guide agent’s actions. pomdp package (Hahsler Cassandra 2025) provides infrastructure define analyze solutions optimal control problems formulated Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDP). package uses solvers pomdp-solve (Cassandra 2015) available companion R package pomdpSolve solve POMDPs using variety exact approximate algorithms. package provides fast functions (using C++, sparse matrix representation, parallelization foreach) perform experiments (sample belief space, simulate trajectories, belief update, calculate regret policy). package also interfaces following algorithms: Enumeration algorithm (Sondik 1971; Monahan 1982). title: Functions for MDP Policies — MDP_policy_functions
text: Implemented functions : q_values_MDP() calculates (approximates) Q-values given model using Bellman optimality equation: $$q(s,) = \sum_{s'} T(s'|s,) [R(s,) + \gamma U(s')]$$ Q-values can used input several functions. MDP_policy_evaluation() evaluates policy \(\pi\) model returns (approximate) state values applying Bellman equation update rule state iteration \(k\): $$U_{k+1}(s) =\sum_a \pi{|s} \sum_{s'} T(s' | s,) [R(s,) + \gamma U_k(s')]$$ iteration, states updated. Updating stopped k_backups iterations largest update \(||U_{k+1} - U_k||_\infty < \theta\). greedy_MDP_action() returns action largest Q-value given state. random_MDP_policy(), manual_MDP_policy(), greedy_MDP_policy() generates different policies. policies can added problem using add_policy().

Tiger)  Tiger <- POMDP(   name = "Tiger Problem",   discount = 0.75,   states = c("tiger-left" , "tiger-right"),   actions = c("listen", "open-left", "open-right"),   observations = c("tiger-left", "tiger-right"),   start = "uniform",    transition_prob = list(     "listen" =     "identity",     "open-left" =  "uniform",     "open-right" = "uniform"   ),    observation_prob = list(     "listen" = rbind(c(0.85, 0.15),                      c(0.15, 0.85)),     "open-left" =  "uniform",     "open-right" = "uniform"   ),    # the reward helper expects: action, start.state, end.state, observation, value   # missing arguments default to NA which matches any value (often denoted as * in POMDPs).   reward = rbind(     R_("listen",                    value =   -1),     R_("open-left",  "tiger-left",  value = -100),     R_("open-left",  "tiger-right", value =   10),     R_("open-right", "tiger-left",  value =   10),     R_("open-right", "tiger-right", value = -100)   ) )  Tiger #> POMDP, list - Tiger Problem #>   Discount factor: 0.75 #>   Horizon: Inf epochs #>   Size: 2 states / 3 actions / 2 obs. #>   Start: uniform #>   Solved: FALSE #>  #>   List components: ‘name’, ‘discount’, ‘horizon’, ‘states’, ‘actions’, #>     ‘observations’, ‘transition_prob’, ‘observation_prob’, ‘reward’, #>     ‘start’, ‘terminal_values’, ‘info’  ### Defining the Tiger problem using functions  trans_f <- function(action, start.state, end.state) {   if(action == 'listen')     if(end.state == start.state) return(1)     else return(0)    return(1/2) ### all other actions have a uniform distribution }  obs_f <- function(action, end.state, observation) {   if(action == 'listen')     if(end.state == observation) return(0.85)   else return(0.15)    return(1/2) }  rew_f <- function(action, start.state, end.state, observation) {   if(action == 'listen') return(-1)   if(action == 'open-left' && start.state == 'tiger-left') return(-100)   if(action == 'open-left' && start.state == 'tiger-right') return(10)   if(action == 'open-right' && start.state == 'tiger-left') return(10)   if(action == 'open-right' && start.state == 'tiger-right') return(-100)   stop('Not possible') }  Tiger_func <- POMDP(   name = "Tiger Problem",   discount = 0.75,   states = c("tiger-left" , "tiger-right"),   actions = c("listen", "open-left", "open-right"),   observations = c("tiger-left", "tiger-right"),   start = "uniform",   transition_prob = trans_f,   observation_prob = obs_f,   reward = rew_f )  Tiger_func #> POMDP, list - After 3 epochs he gets # scared and when a door is opened then he always goes to the other door.  # specify the horizon for each of the two different episodes Tiger_time_dependent <- Tiger Tiger_time_dependent$name <- "Scared Tiger Problem" Tiger_time_dependent$horizon <- c(normal_tiger = 3, scared_tiger = 3) Tiger_time_dependent$transition_prob <- list(   normal_tiger = list(     "listen" = "identity",     "open-left" = "uniform",     "open-right" = "uniform"),   scared_tiger = list(     "listen" = "identity",     "open-left" = rbind(c(0, 1), c(0, 1)),     "open-right" = rbind(c(1, 0), c(1, 0))   ) )

code: data("Tiger") sol <- solve_POMDP(model = Tiger)  # if no start is specified, a uniform belief is used. reward(sol) #> [1] 1.933439  # we have additional information that makes us believe that the tiger # is more likely to the left. reward(sol, belief = c(0.85, 0.15)) #> [1] 3.911252  # we start with strong evidence that the tiger is to the left. reward(sol, belief = "tiger-left") #> [1] 11.45008  # Note that in this case, the total discounted expected reward is greater # than 10 since the tiger problem resets and another game staring with # a uniform belief is played which produces additional reward.  # return reward, the initial node in the policy graph and the optimal action for # two beliefs. reward_node_action(sol, belief = rbind(c(.5, .5), c(.9, .1))) #> $belief #>      tiger-left tiger-right #> [1,]        0.5         0.5 #> [2,]        0.9         0.1 #>  #> $reward #> [1] 1.933439 4.779814 #>  #> $pg_node #> [1] 3 4 #>  #> $action #> [1] listen listen #> Levels: listen open-left open-right #>   # manually combining reward with belief space sampling to show the value function # (color signifies the optimal action) samp <- sample_belief_space(sol, n = 200) rew <- reward_node_action(sol, belief = samp) plot(rew$belief[,"tiger-right"], rew$reward, col = rew$action, ylim = c(0, 15)) legend(x = "top", legend = levels(rew$action), title = "action", col = 1:3, pch = 1)   # this is the piecewise linear value function from the solution plot_value_function(sol, ylim = c(0, 10))
